### 1. Executive summary (source: `docs/company/data/exec-summary.csv`)

**The concept.** NASHA is a planned Indo-Mex brewery and kitchen in Austin, Texas: five core dishes and five core beers designed together so that each plate has a drink chosen for it, with non-alcoholic pairings given equal standing. It is a concept and a development system today, not an operating business.

**The opportunity (a hypothesis).** Hypothesis, untested: guests who already enjoy Indian food, Mexican food and craft beer may value a place where those traditions meet in dishes that feel like one cuisine, with the pairing explained simply. No demand data exists; the cheapest tests are listed in the risk table.

**The solution.** A compact core menu cooked on a small set of stations (fryer, comal, char), a beer list built to match it, and a hall where the brewing is visible. The brewery is the last capital gate: food and demand come first, and host-brewery or collaboration paths can test beer with far less capital.

**The product.** Core 5 food: Chicken 65 Totopos, Paneer Tikka Taco, Goat Birria, Mango Habanero Gobi (appetizer/shareable), Butter Chicken and Roasted Poblano Quesadilla. Core 5 beer: Hefeweizen, Mexican-Style Lager, Vienna Amber, Pilsner, Witbier. All are design briefs; none has been cooked or brewed.

**What may make it different.** The combination and the execution, not any single ingredient: pairing designed in from the start, a no-beef and no-pork kitchen as a clear constraint, and a development process that publishes what failed. Indian, Mexican, fusion, brewery and destination-hospitality businesses all exist in Austin; the market lessons are in the market view.

**Current stage.** Concept and design blueprint, before any physical test. Nothing has been cooked, brewed, tasted by anyone outside the project, priced from real receipts or reviewed by a professional.

**What has been done.** Concept and product system documented; the first home-kitchen test (Chicken 65 Totopos) designed with fixed pass and fail rules and prepared for cooking; economic model structure with provenance rules; operating, kitchen, brewery, guest-journey and space requirements drafted; risk register with cheapest tests; this private site.

**What has not been done.** Nothing has been cooked, brewed, tasted by anyone outside the project, photographed as a real prototype, priced from real receipts or quotes, reviewed by a lawyer, brewer, chef or advisor, or sold. There is no site, no entity, no permit, no customer and no investor conversation.

**Capital strategy.** Staged: pre-capital founder build, low-cost validation, commercial validation, site and design, build, opening. No fundraising amount is set; amounts will follow real quotes. Each stage is tied to the risk it removes and to gates that stop spending when evidence does not support it.

**Next proof points.** Cook and document the first dish with receipts, weights, photographs and tasters' scores; repeat for the other four; compute real food costs; then, once funds exist, take the name to an attorney, scope the legal path for beer with food, and run a first lawful commercial pilot.

**Major risks.** The name is in question (a same-name Austin restaurant has been reported); no dish is proven; margin, labor and throughput are unknown; the brewery is capital-heavy; the founder is the only team member today. Each risk has a cheapest test in the risk table.

**The founder.** Ritesh Mamidi is building NASHA as a one-person project, using the pre-capital period to develop as much of the company as can be done without money: product system, economic model, operating blueprint, a private website and a data room, and personal home-kitchen testing. No hospitality, culinary or brewing credentials are claimed; the capability gaps are listed openly in the future-team view.

**Has not happened.** cooked|brewed|tasted by anyone outside the project|photographed as a real prototype|priced from real receipts or quotes|reviewed by a lawyer, brewer, chef or advisor|sold

**Does not exist.** a site|a legal entity|a permit|a customer|an investor conversation|a named chef, brewer or advisor

### 2. Investor FAQ (`investor-faq.csv`)

**Why Indian x Mexican?** The founder believes the two cuisines share ideas such as flatbreads, chilies and braises. Whether guests find the fusion intentional rather than gimmicky is untested, and cultural advisors have not reviewed it.

**Why beer?** The concept is a brewery and kitchen with drinks chosen for each plate. Beer is the most capital-heavy part, so it is last in the capital order, and partner beer can test the idea first.

**Why Austin?** Austin is the founder's chosen city, and a small desk sample shows taprooms with kitchens and related concepts. That is a hypothesis; demand and room against competitors remain untested.

**Why not start with a food truck?** A truck is a heavy purchase before any dish has passed its gates. The path starts with home cooking, then tastings and a shared kitchen, and a truck is considered only after repeat demand exists.

**Why not contract brew forever?** Contract or partner beer may prove to be enough, and the plan says so. A house brewery is a goal to be justified by evidence, and the change-our-mind file names what would end it.

**Why five dishes?** Five is a focused development set chosen by the founder, not a final menu. A compact menu is a hypothesis for efficient execution, and any dish that fails its gates can be reworked or cut.

**What has actually been tested?** Nothing. No dish has been cooked, no beer brewed, and no guest has tasted anything. What exists is a documented concept, frozen test protocols and a decision model.

**Why should anyone believe the economics?** They should not yet. The economics are a decision model with every input unknown, not a forecast; real receipts, quotes and sales are needed before any figure is meaningful.

**What stops a competitor copying this?** Little, today. Indian-Mexican fusion businesses are already reported in Austin. Any edge would come from execution, pairing design and the process of learning in public, none of which has been tested.

**What happens if NASHA cannot use the name?** A same-name Austin restaurant has been publicly reported, which is a high conflict risk. Counsel has not reviewed it, so the name may be kept, modified or replaced, and brand-independent work continues in the meantime.

**Why hasn't the founder opened already?** The founder has almost no money, so the pre-capital phase is deliberate: build and test what can be done without funds first. Opening needs site, build and licensing capital, and the plan funds each stage only after evidence.

**What exactly would investment fund?** The stages have categories but no amounts: early validation, then legal, IP, pilots and insurance, then site work, build and opening. No raise target is set, and amounts would follow real quotes.

**What is the biggest risk?** That no one has evidence yet: no dish or beer has been tested and no guest has been asked. Name conflict, unknown margins and a capital-heavy brewery follow, each with a cheapest test listed.

### 3. What would change our mind (`change-our-mind.csv`)

| Thesis | What we believe today | Evidence that would change direction | Cheapest way to find out |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FOOD x BEER** | Food and beer designed together is a stronger concept than either alone; untested. | Blind or paired sessions show no lift, or guests value the food alone and treat beer as incidental. | Pairing session with and without matched drinks (H3). |
| **AUSTIN** | Austin is the right first city; supported by a small desk sample only. | Interviews and sales show too small or saturated a niche, or a better-fit city shows clearer demand or access. | Desk refresh then interviews (H6). |
| **CORE 5** | Five dishes are a workable development core; not a final menu. | A dish fails its frozen gates, is gimmicky to blind tasters, or cannot be sourced to D-54. | Cook the sessions and apply the gates. |
| **HEFEWEIZEN as proof beer** | D-77 is an agent proposal awaiting founder confirmation: Hefeweizen as proof beer; unconfirmed. | A brewer finds the style a poor proof, or guests prefer another style for reliability and repeat drinking. | Brewer review of the six proofs. |
| **HOUSE BREWERY** | A house brewery is the long-run goal, last in the capital order. | Guests value partner beer equally; collaboration teaches enough; brewery capex is out of proportion to sales. | Residency or collaboration pilot comparison (H9). |
| **COURT BREWHOUSE** | A concept form, not locked; brewhouse at the centre of a courtyard. | An architect or brewer finds it impractical for the site, drainage, cost or operations. | Architect and brewer review on a candidate site. |
| **PAIRING MODEL** | Each plate has a chosen drink; the logic is a design hypothesis. | Guests ignore the pairing, find it preachy, or choose their own drink with no loss of satisfaction. | Observe orders when pairings are offered or not. |
| **NA EQUAL STANDING** | Non-alcoholic pairings deserve equal standing with beer. | NA drinks prove weaker in tasting, or guests do not order them even with equal billing. | Blind-compare NA pairings with the dishes. |
| **PREMIUM EXPERIENCE** | The experience can justify a premium; no price is known. | Accepted prices do not cover cost per portion, or guests judge the experience ordinary against nearby options. | Small paid tasting with stated willingness to pay (H5). |

### 4. Key assumptions and risks

Every assumption is UNTESTED.

| Assumption | Confidence | Cheapest test | If false |
|---|---|---|---|
| The five beer styles can be brewed to a quality a brewer approves | VERY LOW | Brewer reviews briefs; host-brewery trial batch later | Styles are changed or beer is partner-supplied |
| Labor and waste are modelled correctly in the decision model | VERY LOW | Time real steps; log waste in every session | Contribution turns negative on honest inputs |
| A one-person founder can run early tests without a team | LOW | Run Session 1 to 5 solo and log effort | Tests slow; partners needed sooner |
| A qualified head brewer will join or advise | UNKNOWN | Request a short review of brief and scale framework | Beer path relies on partners only |
| A host brewery would accept a collaboration or residency | UNKNOWN | Ask hosts about collaboration formats | Beer learning waits for capital |
| Brewery scale can be set from real taproom volume | VERY LOW | Brewer sizing analysis | Capex mis-sized |
| The name NASHA can be used in Austin for food and beer | VERY LOW | IP attorney clearance review | Rename or modify; brand spend is wasted |
| Brand-independent work stays reusable if the name changes | LOW | Keep name-dependent assets separate in files | Rework of assets |

The full register (31 assumptions, all UNTESTED) is in `docs/company/data/assumption-register.csv`; the pre-mortem (how NASHA could fail, with early warnings) is in the business model document.

| **PUBLIC RESEARCH** | Indian-Mexican fusion businesses are reported in Austin (T1 summaries, pages not opened): Nasha (reported), Sivestar, Kurry... | NASHA must not claim to be first or only; whether any of these trades today, or has an audience, is unknown. | Founder checks each operator's current status by phone or visit. |
| **PUBLIC RESEARCH** | Austin diners are open to fusion with a clear, named identity. | Openness extends to Indian-Mexican specifically and to a brewery setting. | Short guest interviews on fusion appetite using plain menu cards. |

| **HYPOTHESIS** | Indian diners in Austin want a beer-forward venue with Indian-influenced food. | Enough Indian-dining households see beer and food together as a reason to visit. | Interview Indian-dining households about beer-with-dinner habits. |

| **HYPOTHESIS** | Mexican-dining guests will accept Indian spice logic in a taco or birria format. | Guests rate the result as coherent and tasty, and not as a gimmick. | Blinded tasting of chef-cooked dishes with recruited guests. |
| **PUBLIC RESEARCH** | Experiential venues in Austin draw visits through activity and programming (arcade bar, music, social club). | A food-and-beer story, tours or events can be a reason to visit without an activity hook. | Offer a small tasting-night pop-up and record who attends and why. |
| **HYPOTHESIS** | A designed brewhouse-as-centrepiece hall drives repeat visits in Austin. | Guests return for the room and a lender accepts the capital need in a consolidating market. | Architect and cost review; tour-style pop-up. |

| **HYPOTHESIS** | Guests will choose a venue because of a climate-engineered patio. | Heat discomfort is a real barrier and guests value relief enough to switch venues. | Short interviews plus counts of patio use at several venues across seasons. |
